items.definition: a pain inside your head
exampleSentences: I have a bad headache and need to lie down.
Loud noise always gives me a headache.

items.definition: a pain in your stomach
exampleSentences: She has a stomachache after eating too much.
I got a stomachache from the spicy food.

items.definition: pain or a burning feeling in your throat, often from a cold
exampleSentences: I have a sore throat and it hurts to swallow.
Drink warm tea if you have a sore throat.

items.definition: a body temperature that is higher than normal, often caused by illness
exampleSentences: The child has a fever and needs to rest.
Her fever went down after she took the medicine.

items.definition: a sudden noise you make when air is pushed out of your throat, often because of an illness
exampleSentences: He has a bad cough that keeps him up at night.
Cover your mouth when you cough.

items.definition: a common, mild illness that gives you a runny nose and a sore throat
exampleSentences: I have a cold and can't stop sneezing.
Wear a coat so you don't catch a cold.

items.definition: an area of red spots on your skin, often caused by illness or allergy
exampleSentences: A rash appeared on his arm after he ate the shrimp.
The doctor looked at the rash on my leg.

items.definition: feeling like everything is spinning and you might fall
exampleSentences: I felt dizzy when I stood up too quickly.
She sat down because she was dizzy.

items.definition: bigger than normal because of an injury or illness
exampleSentences: His ankle was swollen after the fall.
Her eyes were swollen from crying.

items.definition: to suddenly push air out through your nose and mouth in a way you cannot control
exampleSentences: She sneezes a lot when spring begins.
Dust always makes me sneeze.

items.definition: an arranged time to see someone, such as a doctor
exampleSentences: I have an appointment with the dentist at three o'clock.
Could I make an appointment for next Monday?

items.definition: the doctor's decision about what illness a patient has
exampleSentences: The doctor's diagnosis was a mild infection.
It took two tests to reach a final diagnosis.

items.definition: a change in your body that shows you might be ill
exampleSentences: A high fever is a common symptom of the flu.
Write down your symptoms before you see the doctor.

items.definition: a piece of paper from a doctor that lets you buy certain medicine
exampleSentences: The doctor gave me a prescription for antibiotics.
You need a prescription to buy this medicine.

items.definition: a shop where you can buy medicine
exampleSentences: I need to pick up my medicine from the pharmacy.
The pharmacy on Main Street is open until nine.

items.definition: medical care that is given to a patient to cure an illness or injury
exampleSentences: The treatment for his infection lasted ten days.
She is receiving treatment at the local hospital.

items.definition: a piece of cloth used to cover and protect an injury
exampleSentences: The nurse put a bandage on my cut.
He wore a bandage around his knee for a week.

items.definition: a medicine that reduces pain
exampleSentences: Take a painkiller if your headache gets worse.
The doctor recommended a mild painkiller.

items.definition: a regular medical examination to make sure you are healthy
exampleSentences: I go for a checkup every year.
The dentist said my next checkup is in six months.

items.definition: the force of blood moving through your body, measured by a doctor
exampleSentences: The nurse checked my blood pressure before the appointment.
High blood pressure can be dangerous if it isn't treated.

items.definition: physical activity that you do to stay fit and healthy
exampleSentences: The doctor told him to get more exercise.
Regular exercise can help lower your blood pressure.

items.definition: the food and drink that a person usually has
exampleSentences: A balanced diet helps your body stay strong.
She changed her diet after she got sick.

items.definition: a period of relaxing or sleeping after being active or ill
exampleSentences: The doctor said I need a lot of rest this week.
Get some rest before you go back to work.

items.definition: a feeling of worry caused by a difficult situation
exampleSentences: Too much stress can make you feel tired all the time.
He tries to reduce stress by walking every evening.

items.definition: to become healthy again after an illness or injury
exampleSentences: It took him a month to recover from the flu.
She is recovering well after the operation.

items.definition: in good physical condition, without illness
exampleSentences: Eating vegetables every day keeps you healthy.
The doctor said the baby is happy and healthy.

items.definition: a natural substance in food that your body needs to stay healthy
exampleSentences: Oranges have a lot of vitamin C.
The doctor suggested I take a vitamin every morning.

items.definition: having a bad physical reaction to something you eat, touch, or breathe
exampleSentences: I'm allergic to peanuts, so I always check the label.
She gets a rash because she's allergic to certain soaps.

items.definition: to suddenly fall down and stop being awake for a short time, for example because of heat or shock
exampleSentences: She felt dizzy and almost fainted in the heat.
He fainted at the sight of blood.

items.definition: damage to a part of your body, often caused by an accident
exampleSentences: He got a knee injury while playing soccer.
The injury kept her out of sports for two months.

lessons.title: Grammar: Should, must and have to

items.definition: how to give advice and talk about obligation and necessity
items.explanationTR:
We use should to give advice or say what is a good idea. It is not very strong.
• You should drink more water when you have a fever.
• You shouldn't stay up too late if you're sick.
We use must for strong obligation, often rules or something the speaker feels is necessary.
• You must take this medicine three times a day.
• Patients must wash their hands before they enter.
We use have to for obligation that comes from outside, like a rule, a doctor, or a situation.
• I have to see a doctor because my cough isn't getting better.
• She has to rest for a week after the operation.
The negative forms are very different in meaning:
• mustn't means it is forbidden - You mustn't stop taking this medicine suddenly.
• don't have to means it isn't necessary - You don't have to worry; it's not serious.
Must never takes -s or 'to': She must rest (not 'She musts rest' or 'She must to rest'). Have to changes with the subject: I have to, she has to.
Use should for friendly advice, must for strong rules or urgent necessity, and have to for obligations that come from outside you.

questions.prompt: You look tired and you have a headache. Maybe you ---- take a painkiller and rest for a while.
questions.explanationTR: 'Maybe you should...' is a very common way to give friendly advice; 'must' is too strong after 'maybe', and 'mustn't' or 'don't have to' give the wrong meaning.

questions.prompt: This is a hospital rule: all visitors ---- wear a mask in this ward.
questions.explanationTR: 'Must' shows a strict rule that everyone has to follow; 'should' would only be advice, not a hospital rule.

questions.prompt: My cough isn't getting better, so I ---- make an appointment with my doctor.
questions.explanationTR: 'Have to' expresses a necessity caused by the situation, since the cough isn't improving; 'don't have to' would mean it isn't necessary, which contradicts the context.

questions.prompt: The doctor said, "You ---- stop taking this medicine suddenly; it can be dangerous."
questions.explanationTR: 'Mustn't' means it is forbidden, which fits a dangerous action to avoid; 'should' (without 'not') would wrongly recommend stopping suddenly, the opposite of the warning.

questions.prompt: The doctor said the results are fine, so you ---- come back for a follow-up appointment.
questions.explanationTR: 'Don't have to' means coming back isn't necessary, which fits normal results; 'shouldn't' would suggest something negative about returning, which doesn't match good news.

questions.prompt: If the pain doesn't go away tomorrow, I think you ---- call the clinic, just to be safe.
questions.explanationTR: 'Should' fits a personal opinion given as gentle advice, shown by 'I think' and 'just to be safe'; 'have to' and 'must' would state a firm necessity, which is stronger than the sentence intends.

questions.prompt: My brother broke his leg, so he ---- stay at home for six weeks.
questions.explanationTR: With he/she/it, 'have to' becomes 'has to'. 'Must' and 'should' are never followed by 'to', and 'is having' is not used for obligation.

questions.prompt: Because of my allergy, I ---- carry my medicine with me at all times.
questions.explanationTR: 'Have to' shows a necessity that comes from an outside situation, here the allergy; 'don't have to' would mean the opposite, that it isn't necessary.

items.definition: a short conversation at a doctor's office and seven questions about what to say

questions.prompt:
Doctor: "What seems to be the problem today?"
Patient: "----"
Doctor: "How long have you had it?"
options: I have a headache and a fever.
I'd like to pay by credit card.
I already took my vitamins today.
My appointment is at three o'clock.
questions.explanationTR: Only this option describes a health problem, which answers the doctor's question and fits the follow-up about how long it has lasted.

questions.prompt:
Doctor: "I'm going to check your blood pressure and look at your throat."
Patient: "Okay. ----"
Doctor: "Try to relax; it will only take a minute."
options: I bought this medicine at the pharmacy.
I'm a little nervous about it.
My last checkup was a year ago.
I need a prescription for painkillers.
My blood pressure is usually low.
questions.explanationTR: 'I'm a little nervous' explains why the doctor tells the patient to relax; the other replies give information but don't show a feeling that needs calming.

questions.prompt:
Doctor: "Your test results show a mild infection, but nothing serious."
Patient: "That's a relief. ----"
Doctor: "Yes, take one tablet every eight hours for a week."
options: How did I get this infection?
Do I need any medicine for it?
When should I come back to see you?
Is the pharmacy open on Sundays?
questions.explanationTR: The doctor says 'Yes' and explains how to take tablets, so the patient asked about medicine; 'Is the infection very serious?' is wrong because the doctor already said it isn't.

questions.prompt:
Doctor: "Do you have any allergies I should know about?"
Patient: "----"
Doctor: "Good, then this medicine should be safe for you."
options: Yes, I'm allergic to some medicines.
My throat has been sore since Monday.
I usually go to bed at eleven.
No, I'm not allergic to anything.
I have a checkup scheduled for Friday.
questions.explanationTR: The doctor's response, 'Good, then this medicine should be safe,' only makes sense after hearing there are no allergies; an allergy to some medicines would make the doctor careful, not pleased.

questions.prompt:
Patient: "I've had a stomachache since yesterday, and I feel a bit dizzy."
Doctor: "----"
Patient: "Yes, right after lunch."
options: How long have you felt dizzy?
Did it start after you ate something?
questions.explanationTR: 'Yes, right after lunch' tells us when the problem started, so the doctor asked if it began after eating; 'How long have you felt dizzy?' cannot be answered with 'Yes'.

questions.prompt:
Doctor: "You should rest for a few days and drink plenty of water."
Patient: "----"
Doctor: "If the fever doesn't go down by Friday, come back and see me."
options: And what if I don't get better?
How much water should I drink?
Do you know a good pharmacy nearby?
Do I need a prescription for that?
Can I go back to the gym now?
questions.explanationTR: The doctor's reply about coming back if the fever doesn't go down answers the question 'what if I don't get better?'; it doesn't answer questions about water, a pharmacy, a prescription or the gym.

questions.prompt:
Receptionist: "The doctor is ready for you now."
Patient: "----"
Receptionist: "Just through that door on the right."
options: Thank you. Where's the nearest pharmacy?
Thank you. Which room should I go to?
Thank you. Can I borrow a pen?
Thank you. Is the bill ready yet?
Thank you. What time is my next appointment?
questions.explanationTR: The receptionist's reply about 'through that door on the right' answers a question about which room to go to.
